title: Peter of Saint Joseph: aid as being and as benefit
source_text: CXXXIII. Quibus similia tradit Petrus a Sancto Joseph in fine disputationis septimae tractatus de gratia divina. Auxilium divinum, inquit, duobus modis spectari potest, vel in genere entis, vel in genere beneficii. Si priori modo spectetur, fieri potest ut unus cum aequali, aut etiam cum majori auxilio non convertatur, & alter convertatur cum minori. Ratio est, quia cum gratia non determinet voluntatem, oblato duobus hominibus aequali auxilio in ratione entis, uterque manet indifferens ad consentiendum, aut non consentiendum. Quare unus illorum libere poterit consentire, etsi alter minime consentiat. Si vero auxilium spectetur sub ratione doni, & beneficii, tunc fieri non potest ut posito aequali auxilio, unus convertatur, non alter; quia auxilia tunc dicuntur aequalia in ratione beneficii, quando aeque prosunt: quare si unum ita prosit, ut reipsa effectum habeat, aliud minime, jam in genere beneficii aequalia non sunt.
pass_a_gloss: CXXXIII. Things like these Peter of Saint Joseph teaches at the end of the seventh disputation of the treatise on divine grace. The divine aid, he says, can be regarded in two ways, either in the genus of being, or in the genus of benefit. If it be regarded in the former way, it can happen that one is not converted with equal, or even with greater aid, & another is converted with less. The reason is, because since grace does not determine the will, equal aid in the character of being being offered to two men, each remains indifferent to consenting, or not consenting. Wherefore one of them will be able freely to consent, though the other in no way consents. But if the aid be regarded under the character of gift, & benefit, then it cannot happen that equal aid being posited, one is converted, not the other; because aids are then called equal in the character of benefit, when they profit equally: wherefore if one so profits, that it in fact has effect, the other not at all, they are already not equal in the genus of benefit.
pass_b_english: Thesis CXXXIII. Peter of Saint Joseph teaches much the same at the end of the seventh disputation of his treatise on divine grace. 'Divine aid,' he says, 'can be viewed in two ways: as a being or as a benefit. Viewed the first way, it can happen that one person is not converted with equal or even greater aid while another is converted with less. The reason is that grace does not determine the will; when equal aid, considered as a being, is offered to two people, each stays undetermined between consenting and not consenting, so one of them may freely consent though the other does not consent at all.

But if the aid is viewed as a gift and benefit, it cannot happen that, given equal aid, one is converted and the other not. For aids are called equal in the order of benefit when they benefit equally; so if one aid benefits to the point of actually taking effect and the other not at all, they are already unequal in the order of benefit.'
